title: Immunoassay Labels: From Insulin RIA to Chemiluminescence, ECLIA and the HBsAg Cutoff Index
summary: Trace immunoassay labels from Yalow and Berson’s insulin radioimmunoassay to chemiluminescent and electrochemiluminescent (ECLIA) detection, and read a qualitative HBsAg cutoff index correctly.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 45 Hits 9, 13 and 14, checked against Ahsan 2022, Cinquanta 2017, Zhang 2019, Vogeser 2014, Park 2021, Lee 2023, Zhang 2022 and Wang 2022. Qualifications: the reviewer’s HBsAg CL-EIA cutoff of “0.5 mIU/mL (8.0 SD above the mean of HBsAg-negative specimens)” was not found; the assays read report a signal-to-cutoff index whose IU/mL equivalent is assay-specific (about 0.040 IU/mL at index 1.0 for one qualitative assay; below 0.050 IU/mL negative for one quantitative ECLIA), so the lesson teaches the index and its retest/confirm logic (flag f-hbsag-cutoff-assay-specific). Pending, not taught as fact: the reviewer’s “~5 pg/mL” RIA and “~0.1 pg/mL” chemiluminescent sensitivity figures (sources state only that chemiluminescence is more sensitive), and the “gold electrode” surface (sources read say only “the electrode”). ECLIA emission is taught as about 620 nm; one review gives 642 nm. Not taught: Hits 10, 11 and 12, and the Number Vault table.

objectives: Describe the first radioimmunoassay (Yalow and Berson, insulin), its isotope labels and why its use declined.
Distinguish direct and indirect chemiluminescent labels and state their sensitivity advantage over RIA.
Explain how an ECLIA produces light with a ruthenium label, tripropylamine and an electrode.
Interpret a qualitative HBsAg signal-to-cutoff index, including initially and repeatedly reactive results.

scenes.title: Click, glow, or switch?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three questions at an immunoassay bench. (1) A trainee finds an old insulin kit that uses a radioactive label and asks why labs moved away from it. (2) The new analyzer’s light is produced only when a voltage is applied to an electrode. (3) A first HBsAg screen on an automated chemiluminescent analyzer reports an index of 1.6 against a cutoff of 1.0. Question token: “Label, light, or cutoff?”

cues.text: Three questions at the immunoassay bench. A trainee finds an old insulin kit with a radioactive label and asks why labs moved on.
The new analyzer makes its light only when a voltage is applied to an electrode.
And a first hepatitis B surface antigen screen reads an index of 1.6 against a cutoff of 1.0. Is each one about the label, the light, or the cutoff?

scenes.title: Radioimmunoassay: the first immunoassay
scenes.altText: Schematic: radioimmunoassay (RIA). Card 1: Yalow and Berson used radiolabelled insulin to measure insulin in human plasma (Nature report 1959; full paper in J Clin Invest 1960); RIA replaced bioassays and precipitation tests. Card 2: isotopes used include iodine-125, tritium (³H), carbon-14 and phosphorus-32, counted with a radiation counter. Card 3: principle: labelled and unlabelled antigen compete for a limited amount of specific antibody. Card 4: limits: isotope half-life, radioactive waste disposal, specialised instruments and trained staff.

cues.text: Radioimmunoassay was the first immunoassay. Yalow and Berson used radiolabelled insulin to measure insulin in human plasma, reported in 1959, with the full paper in 1960.
Labels include iodine-125, tritium, carbon-14 and phosphorus-32, and the radiation is counted. RIA replaced older bioassays and precipitation tests.
The classic design is competitive: labelled antigen and the patient’s unlabelled antigen compete for a limited amount of antibody.
RIA is sensitive and inexpensive, but it is limited by the isotope’s half-life, radioactive waste, special instruments and trained staff.

scenes.title: Chemiluminescence and ECLIA
scenes.altText: Chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA) card: the label is a light-emitting molecule. Direct labels: acridinium esters and ruthenium complexes. Indirect (enzyme) labels: alkaline phosphatase with the dioxetane substrate AMPPD, or horseradish peroxidase with luminol plus an enhancer. Reported analytic sensitivity is superior to RIA, ELISA and fluoroenzyme methods; automated CLIA runs in about 30 to 40 minutes. ECLIA card: tris(bipyridine)ruthenium(II) label, Ru(bpy)₃²⁺, with tripropylamine (TPA) coreactant; biotinylated antibody binds streptavidin magnetic microparticles; a magnet captures them on the electrode in the measuring cell; unbound material is washed away; a voltage on the electrode triggers emission at about 620 nm, measured by a photomultiplier.

cues.text: Chemiluminescent immunoassays use a label that emits light. Direct labels include acridinium esters and ruthenium complexes; indirect labels are enzymes, such as alkaline phosphatase with a dioxetane substrate, or peroxidase with luminol and an enhancer.
Their analytic sensitivity is reported to be superior to RIA and ELISA, with a wide dynamic range, low background and automated runs of about thirty to forty minutes.

Electrochemiluminescence, ECLIA, uses a ruthenium bipyridine label with tripropylamine as coreactant. The immune complex is bound to streptavidin magnetic microparticles, and a magnet captures them on the electrode in the measuring cell.

Unbound material is washed away. Then a voltage on the electrode triggers light at about six hundred and twenty nanometres, read by a photomultiplier. The light is started by electrochemistry, not by simply mixing reagents.

scenes.title: Reading an HBsAg cutoff index
scenes.altText: Result ladder for one qualitative chemiluminescent HBsAg assay, as described in one hospital study: result is a signal-to-cutoff index; index below 1.0 = nonreactive; index 1.0 or above = initially reactive; in that laboratory, results from 1 to 50 were retested in duplicate, and if 2 of 3 results were 1.0 or above the sample was repeatedly reactive and went to a confirmatory assay; above 50, no further testing per the manufacturer. Cutoff in IU/mL is assay-specific: about 0.040 IU/mL at index 1.0 for the qualitative assay; a quantitative ECLIA called results below 0.050 IU/mL negative. Hook answers: (1) RIA was replaced because of isotope handling, waste and instruments, and chemiluminescence is more sensitive; (2) that is ECLIA, light started at the electrode; (3) index 1.6 is initially reactive, so repeat and confirm.

cues.text: Qualitative HBsAg chemiluminescent assays report an index: the sample signal divided by the cutoff. Below 1.0 is nonreactive; 1.0 or above is only initially reactive.

In one hospital study, indexes from 1 to 50 were retested in duplicate. Two of three at 1.0 or above made the sample repeatedly reactive, and a confirmatory assay followed. What the index 1.0 equals in IU per millilitre depends on the assay.
Back to the hook. RIA gave way because of isotope handling, waste and special instruments, and chemiluminescence is more sensitive.
The analyzer that lights on a voltage is an ECLIA. And an HBsAg index of 1.6 is initially reactive: repeat it, then confirm.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “RIA was dropped because it was insensitive” (✓ RIA is sensitive; isotope half-life, waste and special instruments were the limits, and chemiluminescence is reported to be more sensitive still); “ECLIA light starts when reagents are mixed” (✓ ECLIA light is started by electrochemistry at the electrode surface after a voltage is applied); “HBsAg index ≥ 1.0 on the first run = confirmed infection” (✓ it is initially reactive; repeat testing and a confirmatory assay follow, and the IU/mL cutoff is assay-specific).

cues.text: Trap one: RIA was dropped because it was insensitive. No: RIA is sensitive. Its limits were isotopes, waste and special instruments.
Trap two: ECLIA light starts when reagents are mixed. No: the light starts at the electrode surface when a voltage is applied.
Trap three: a first HBsAg index of 1.0 or more is a confirmed infection. No: it is initially reactive. Repeat it, then confirm.

scenes.title: Click, glow, switch
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “RIA CLICKS (radiation is counted), CLIA GLOWS (a chemical reaction makes light), ECLIA has a SWITCH (a voltage at the electrode turns the light on). And a cutoff index of 1 is a doorbell, not a verdict.” Tokens: click = RIA · glow = CLIA · switch = ECLIA. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: RIA clicks, because radiation is counted. CLIA glows, because a chemical reaction makes light. ECLIA has a switch: a voltage at the electrode turns the light on. And an index of 1 is a doorbell, not a verdict.

Where it breaks: click stands for counting radiation, not a sound; ECLIA still needs its tripropylamine chemistry, not just electricity; and sensitivity depends on the whole assay design, not the label alone.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “RIA: Yalow and Berson, insulin, isotopes → replaced by more sensitive chemiluminescence”, “ECLIA: ruthenium + TPA, voltage at electrode · HBsAg index ≥ 1.0 = initially reactive → repeat, confirm”.

cues.text: Radioimmunoassay began with insulin but needs isotopes, chemiluminescent labels are more sensitive, ECLIA starts its ruthenium light with a voltage at the electrode, and a first HBsAg index of 1 or more is only initially reactive until repeated and confirmed.

props.label: RIA: insulin, isotopes → chemiluminescence more sensitive
ECLIA: Ru + TPA, voltage · HBsAg index ≥ 1 → repeat, confirm

explanation.what: Plain language: every immunoassay needs a tag that shows where the antibody has bound. The first tag was radioactive; modern analyzers use tags that make light, either from a chemical reaction or, in electrochemiluminescence, when a voltage is applied at an electrode. A qualitative result is then reported as how far the signal sits above a cutoff. Scientific terms: radioimmunoassay (RIA), iodine-125, tritium, competitive binding, chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA), acridinium ester, alkaline phosphatase, adamantyl dioxetane (AMPPD), horseradish peroxidase, luminol, enhancer, electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA), tris(bipyridine)ruthenium(II), tripropylamine (TPA), streptavidin magnetic microparticles, photomultiplier, signal-to-cutoff index (S/CO, COI), initially reactive, repeatedly reactive, confirmatory assay.
explanation.why: RIA measures radiation, so it depends on isotope half-life, waste disposal and special instruments. Chemiluminescent labels give strong signal over low background without radioactivity, which supports automation and high sensitivity. In ECLIA the light reaction is started electrochemically at the electrode, which makes it easier to control. A single result just above a cutoff can be falsely reactive, so screening assays retest and confirm before a sample is called positive.
explanation.measure: RIA labels: ¹²⁵I, ³H, ¹⁴C, ³²P. CLIA: direct (acridinium, ruthenium) or indirect (ALP + AMPPD; HRP + luminol + enhancer); automated runs about 30–40 min. ECLIA: Ru(bpy)₃²⁺ + TPA; magnetic capture on the electrode, wash, voltage, emission about 620 nm read by photomultiplier; a competitive ECLIA gives an inverse calibration curve. HBsAg qualitative index: < 1.0 nonreactive; ≥ 1.0 initially reactive; repeat in duplicate, 2 of 3 ≥ 1.0 = repeatedly reactive → confirmatory assay; IU/mL equivalent of the cutoff is assay-specific.
explanation.differs: RIA (radiation counted) vs CLIA (chemical reaction makes light) vs ECLIA (voltage at the electrode starts the light reaction); direct vs indirect chemiluminescent labels; initially reactive vs repeatedly reactive vs confirmed.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the analyte of the first RIA, identify the ruthenium/TPA label system of ECLIA and what triggers its light, rank label systems by sensitivity, or choose the next step for an HBsAg index just above 1.0.

comparisons.title: CLIA vs ECLIA

right.label: ECLIA
points: Started by voltage at the electrode

comparisons.distinguisher: How the light reaction is started: mixing reagents vs electrochemistry at an electrode.

mnemonic.text: RIA CLICKS (radiation is counted), CLIA GLOWS (a chemical reaction makes light), ECLIA has a SWITCH (a voltage at the electrode turns the light on). A cutoff index of 1 is a doorbell, not a verdict.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates the three label systems by how the signal is made, and reminds that an index just above 1.0 needs follow-up.
mnemonic.limitation: “Click” stands for counting radiation, not a sound; ECLIA still depends on its tripropylamine coreactant chemistry; sensitivity depends on the whole assay design, not the label alone; cutoff rules are assay-specific.

analogyLimitations: Measuring-cell and label drawings are schematic.
The HBsAg retest ladder follows one hospital study and one manufacturer’s rules; other assays and laboratories differ.
takeaway: Radioimmunoassay began with insulin but needs isotopes, chemiluminescent labels are more sensitive, ECLIA starts its ruthenium light with a voltage at the electrode, and a first HBsAg index of 1 or more is only initially reactive until repeated and confirmed.

questions.stem: Yalow and Berson developed the first radioimmunoassay in the late 1950s. Which analyte did it measure?

options.rationale: Correct. They used radiolabelled insulin to measure plasma insulin, reported in 1959 and in full in 1960.
Incorrect. The first RIA measured insulin, not TSH.
Incorrect. The first RIA measured insulin in plasma, not a urine pregnancy hormone.
Incorrect. The first RIA was a hormone assay for insulin, not an infectious-disease antigen.

questions.stem: In an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) with a ruthenium-complex label, what starts the light emission that the photomultiplier measures?

options.text: A voltage applied to the electrode, with tripropylamine as coreactant
options.rationale: Correct. Magnetic microparticles carrying the complex are captured on the electrode, washed, and a voltage starts the Ru(bpy)₃²⁺/TPA light reaction.

options.text: Simply mixing the label with trigger or substrate reagents in solution
options.rationale: Incorrect. Light started by mixing reagents describes chemical chemiluminescence (CLEIA); in ECLIA the reaction is initiated electrochemically on the electrode surface.

options.text: Excitation of the label by a laser beam
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is fluorescence; ECLIA needs no light source to excite the label.
Incorrect. That is RIA; ECLIA labels are not radioactive.

questions.stem: A first HBsAg screen on a qualitative chemiluminescent analyzer gives an index of 1.6 (cutoff index 1.0). Under the laboratory rules in which equivocal indexes are retested, what is the best next step?

options.text: Retest in duplicate; if 2 of 3 results are ≥ 1.0, send for a confirmatory assay
options.rationale: Correct. An index ≥ 1.0 is initially reactive; a repeatedly reactive sample is then confirmed.

options.text: Report as confirmed hepatitis B infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single result just above the cutoff is only initially reactive and can be falsely reactive.

options.text: Report as nonreactive because the index is below 5
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nonreactive means an index below 1.0.

options.text: Convert the index to 0.5 mIU/mL and report that value
options.rationale: Incorrect. A qualitative index is not a concentration, and the IU/mL equivalent of the cutoff is assay-specific.

claims.text: RIA was the first immunoassay: Yalow and Berson measured plasma insulin with radiolabelled insulin (1959 report, 1960 full paper); isotopes ¹²⁵I, ³H, ¹⁴C, ³²P; competitive binding; replaced bioassays and precipitation tests; limited by half-life, waste, instruments and trained staff.

CLIA direct labels (acridinium, ruthenium) and indirect labels (ALP + AMPPD, HRP + luminol + enhancer); sensitivity superior to RIA, ELISA and FEIA; wide range, low background, automated 30–40 min runs.

ECLIA: Ru(bpy)₃²⁺ label with TPA coreactant; streptavidin magnetic microparticles captured on the electrode; wash; voltage starts emission read by photomultiplier; started electrochemically rather than by mixing; competitive ECLIA gives an inverse curve.

claims.note: Zhang 2019 gives 642 nm for the Ru(bpy)₃²⁺/TPA system; the lesson says “about 620 nm”.

claims.text: Qualitative HBsAg index: < 1.0 nonreactive, ≥ 1.0 initially reactive; duplicate retest, 2 of 3 ≥ 1.0 repeatedly reactive, then confirmatory assay; IU/mL equivalent of the cutoff is assay-specific (about 0.040 IU/mL at index 1.0 for one assay; < 0.050 IU/mL negative for one quantitative ECLIA).
claims.note: The retest ladder is one laboratory’s protocol with one manufacturer’s rules.

claims.text: RIA sensitivity “~5 pg/mL” and CL-EIA “~0.1 pg/mL”; ECLIA light emitted at a “gold” electrode surface; HBsAg CL-EIA cutoff “0.5 mIU/mL (8.0 SD above the mean of HBsAg-negative specimens)”.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 45 Hit 14 gives the HBsAg CL-EIA cutoff as 0.5 mIU/mL (8.0 SD above the HBsAg-negative mean). The assays read report a signal-to-cutoff index with an assay-specific IU/mL equivalent: manufacturer data of about 0.040 IU/mL (40 mIU/mL) at the 1.0 index cutoff for one qualitative CLIA, and < 0.050 IU/mL negative for one quantitative ECLIA (Lee 2023). The lesson teaches the index and retest/confirm logic, not a single universal cutoff (register flag rv-hbsag-cutoff-assay-specific).
